title: Robbers Cave
text:
In the summer of 1954, Muzafer Sherif and his colleagues ran a summer camp at Robbers Cave State Park in Oklahoma. The campers were 22 eleven-year-old boys, chosen to be similar in background, who did not know each other. They arrived in two separate groups and, at first, did not know the other group existed. Each group bonded, chose a name (the Rattlers and the Eagles) and developed its own customs.

Then the staff let the groups discover each other and set up a tournament of baseball, tug of war and other contests with prizes for the winners. Rivalry quickly turned to hostility: name-calling, a burned flag, raids on each other's cabins.

Simply bringing the groups together for meals or films did not help; those meetings turned into food fights and insults. What worked was a series of problems neither group could solve alone, which the staff arranged. The camp's water supply failed and all the boys had to search the pipeline. They pooled money to rent a film. When a truck bringing food would not start, they hauled it together with the same rope they had used for tug of war. By the end, most boys chose to ride home on one bus.
lesson: Contact alone rarely heals a rivalry between groups. Give them a real goal that neither side can reach without the other, and let them work on it side by side.
people: Muzafer Sherif, Carolyn Sherif, O. J. Harvey, B. Jack White, William Hood
location: Robbers Cave State Park, Oklahoma, USA
source: Sherif, M., Harvey, O. J., White, B. J., Hood, W. R., and Sherif, C. W. (1961). Intergroup Conflict and Cooperation: The Robbers Cave Experiment. University of Oklahoma Book Exchange.
caveat: Archival research, notably by Gina Perry, has shown that staff steered events more than the published account suggests and that an earlier 1953 version of the study collapsed.
